extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and general readers of comparative mythology
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook-style survey and classification of creation (cosmogonic) myths and related myth-types from many cultures, intended to present primary tales and parallels before comparing likenesses and differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground comparative analysis in primary instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Before speculating upon the reason for the similarity between cosmogonic myths in all parts of the globe ... we shall find it profitable to study the chief creation tales themselves, so that when we come to discuss their likeness or unlikeness we shall be well furnished with examples in support of the views we adopt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescriptive methodological advice: collect and cite copious parallels/instances from primary tales prior to theorizing; treat quotations/instances as 'ready armour' useful both offensively and defensively in argument. Anti-pattern: theorizing about likeness/unlikeness without being 'well furnished and abundantly fortified with instances.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of cosmogony
rubrics_metrics.description: Cosmogony is the effort to account for the origin of Heaven and earth and all that is in them — literally 'world-birth' (Greek cosmos + gignesthai).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the term 'cosmogony' to frame study of creation myths; treat it as the central rubric when organizing creation narratives and comparative discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soul myths
rubrics_metrics.description: Myths in which a person's life, heart, or soul may be separated from him as a life-token or life-index, and so long as this is kept safe the owner is immortal; and other myths dealing with the passage of the soul to the Otherworld.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given (Egyptians: Story of the two brothers; Hebrews: Samson and Delilah; Greeks: Meleager; Cingalese: Thossakin; Eskimos: Kujanguak; universal belief in birth-trees). When classifying, note both the life-token motif and variants about soul passage to the Otherworld.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fire myths
rubrics_metrics.description: Myths in which the world is destroyed by fire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Roman (Seneca), Hebrew (Biblical belief), Teutons/Scandinavia (Völuspá), Algonquins (Michabo), Aztecs (fifty-two year cycle and new fire ritual), Maya, Peruvians (eclipse/consuming flame), Tupi-Guarani. Use this category for motifs of destruction-by-fire and renewal; note ritual or calendrical ties (e.g., Aztec new-fire ceremony).

rubrics_metrics.name: Flood myths
rubrics_metrics.description: A great deluge in which Heaven or the earth or both are submerged and all living things drowned except one individual or family favoured by the god(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Egyptians (Tem, Temu), Babylonians (Ut-Napishtim), Hebrews (Noah), Persians (Yima), Greeks (Deucalion), Teutons (Bergelmir), Hindus (Manu), and many indigenous examples worldwide. When identifying flood myths, look for a single surviving human/lineage and divine favour as central motifs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Myths of a place of reward
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditions that posit a celestial garden or abode of bliss for the good (e.g., Aalu, Alburz, Elysian Fields, Fortunate Isles, Valhalla, Nirvana, Happy hunting grounds, Tlalocan, Bolotu).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 'place of reward' dimension to map cultural conceptions of paradise; accompanying attributes (presiding deities, landscape features, inhabitants) are important for comparative mapping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Myths of a place of punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditions naming an underworld or site of punishment (e.g., Egyptian Amenti, Babylonian Sheol/Aralu, Greek Tartarus/Hades, Celtic Annwn, Teutonic Hel, Japanese Yomi, Maya Xibalba, Mexican Mictlan).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When cataloguing, record both the place-name and presiding deity/deities, and note transformations (e.g., bad men becoming animals, slaves, marmots, coyotes) as culturally specific punitive motifs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Myths of journeys/adventures through the Underworld
rubrics_metrics.description: Narratives of descent into, travel through, or return from the Underworld or place of the dead (e.g., Osiris, Ishtar's descent, Orpheus and Eurydice, Persephone, Psyche, Alcestis, Harrying of Hell, Izanagi's descent, Kiches of Guatemala).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify as a motif complex involving descent, trial, rescue or failure; useful for analyzing notions of death, afterlife, and boundary-crossing. Note episodic examples and variants across cultures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Food of the dead formula
rubrics_metrics.description: An individual 'dies' or is kidnapped, goes to the Otherworld, and having partaken of the food there is unable to return to earth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Babylonian Adapa (refuses food of life), Greek Persephone, Finns (Kalevala), Chinooks (shamanistic practice). Use this formula to identify narratives where consumption in the Otherworld creates permanence of death/otherness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sun myths
rubrics_metrics.description: Myths centered on solar deities or figures who embody or are associated with the sun (e.g., Egyptians Ra and Horus; Accadians Amar-utuki; Babylonians Merodach and Shamash; Greeks Apollo/Helios and Phaethon; Celts Lug; Hindus Agni; Aztecs Piltzintecutli).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record principal solar figures and their attributed roles (life-force, provider of material force, sacrificial dependence) and note cosmological linkages (e.g., sun as source/consumer of offerings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moon myths
rubrics_metrics.description: Myths closely associated with flood myths; the moon is often goddess of water, dampness, rain and is linked with death, cold, sleep and miasma. Many myths attribute deluges to the moon or see moon and water as mythical mothers of the human race.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Egyptian Isis; Babylonian Sin; Greek Selene; Roman Luna/Diana; Algonquins (moon = night/death/cold/sleep/water); Aztecs (Citatli/Atl conflation). Pay attention to cultural conflations of moon and water and lunar roles in sickness/childbirth/harvest motifs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Star myths
rubrics_metrics.description: Beliefs that stars are metamorphosed men, women, beasts, ancestors or gods; the good at death may become stars (e.g., Egyptians, Babylonians, Greeks — Pleiades, Castor and Pollux; Hindus, Bushmen, North American tribes, Mexicans, Peruvians, Eskimos).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use star myths to trace ancestor/hero deification and cosmological mapping; note specific constellation-identifications (Pleiades as girls, Ursa Major as bear, Venus as Quetzalcoatl) as useful comparative markers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ætiological myths (myths to account for customs or rites)
rubrics_metrics.description: Myths that explain the origin or reason for a custom, rite, festival or sacred object (e.g., Dionysus and Pentheus explaining the festival; Kikuyus explaining sacrifices to Ngai; Todas explaining dairyman sacrifices; Blackfeet sun-dance; Pawnee skull-dance; Wiradthuri bull-roarer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify myths by their explanatory function for ritual practice or social custom; when using ætiologies, link narrative elements to the contemporary or historical ritual they purport to justify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present variant, culture-specific cosmogonies before comparative claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The chapter proceeds to present detailed, culture-specific creation stories (Indian, Egyptian, Babylonian, Chinese, Hebrew, Japanese, Iranian, Celtic, Norse, Mexican/Aztec) before raising questions of influence, similarity or difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizational guideline: when writing or teaching comparative cosmogony, present each culture's account (including variant versions within a tradition) in detail — e.g., Purusha, Satapatha Brahmana, Vishnu Purana in Indian materials; Neb-er-tcher and Osiris variants in Egyptian materials — before attempting cross-cultural comparison or claims of borrowing/influence.
